newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's defence minister calls off U.S. trip.
newsitem.headline: Russia's defence minister calls off U.S. trip.

text.p: Russia's defence minister Igor Rodionov, embroiled in controversy over the sacking of one of his top generals, hurriedly called off a visit to the United States on Tuesday.

The U.S. embassy in Moscow said it had not yet been informed of the decision, but a defence ministry spokesman told Reuters that a report by Interfax news agency that Rodionov's trip was off was correct.
The Kremlin earlier publicly distanced itself from Rodionov's handling of the removal of General Vladimir Semyonov, 56, commander of land forces since 1991.
Semyonov, by his own account, was called in by Rodionov on Friday and told he faced unspecified misconduct charges.
On Monday the ministry told the press Semyonov had been sacked "for actions which discredit the honour and dignity of a serviceman and are incompatible with his post".
But a spokesman for President Boris Yeltsin said the ministry had jumped the gun.

Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had agreed to Rodionov's request to suspend Semyonov but would not sign his dismissal decree until the case had been considered by a presidential committee on military appointments.
"This decree does not exist," Yastrzhembsky told a regular Kremlin briefing, pointedly dissociating the Kremlin from the accusation of misconduct against Semyonov.
Yastrzhembsky said all questions about what he called "this strong formulation" should be addressed to the Defence Ministry. "Somebody was trying to anticipate events," he added.
"I have not agreed to quit whatever the formulation is," Interfax quoted a defiant Semyonov as saying on Tuesday. "I intend to defend my honour and reputation to the end."
He described the misconduct charge as another attempt to mislead the president and said he had written to Yeltsin to defend himself.

Rodionov, a career officer who replaced the unpopular Pavel Grachev in July as minister, has often shown an uncertain touch and has made contradictory statements on the state of the armed forces and on Russia's attitude to NATO expansion.
His visit to Washington from December 4 to 8 would have returned a trip which Defence Secretary William Perry made to Moscow in October.

General Semyonov told Izvestia newspaper he had been called in by Rodionov on Friday and told he was being sacked because of serious allegations about unspecified "commercial activities" of his wife, who works in the Moscow office of Rosvertol, a Russian helicopter manufacturer.
Russian commentators were sceptical of this argument but were mostly unable to come up with a better explanation for Semyonov's removal.

Interfax news agency quoted Semyonov as saying on Tuesday he had still not been presented with concrete allegations of misconduct and disagreed strongly with the grounds given by the ministry for his removal.
He told Izvestia he would try to clear his name in court.
The row over Semyonov, a well-qualified and apparently respected officer, is the latest morale-sapping blow to hit the once proud Russian army.
Officers are angry over poor living standards and unpaid wages, and over the humiliation suffered by the army at the hands of lightly-armed Chechen rebels.
President Yeltsin last month agreed to withdraw the last Russian soldiers from Chechnya as part of the price of ending Russia's disastrous 21-month campaign there.
Rodionov was appointed in July on the recommendation of now ousted security supremo Alexander Lebed. He was formerly head of the General Staff Academy.
